sections.body_md:
A quadratic is the function a symmetric matrix, a linear term, and a constant can build: one half of \(x^T A x\), plus \(b^T x\), plus \(c\). The one half is a bookkeeping choice. It makes the gradient equal to \(A x + b\) and the Hessian equal to \(A\), with no extra factor of two to carry around. If a model is handed to you with an unsymmetric matrix, replace that matrix by its symmetric part before doing anything else. The function does not change.

Stationarity is the linear system \(A x = -b\). When \(A\) is positive definite the system has one solution, the function is strictly convex and coercive, and that solution is the unique global minimizer. The minimum value is \(c\) minus one half of \(b^T A^{-1} b\).

When \(A\) is only positive semidefinite the function is still convex, and a minimizer exists exactly when \(-b\) lies in the column space of \(A\). If it does, the solutions form an affine subspace parallel to the null space, and they all share one value. If it does not, the linear term points into a flat direction and the function is unbounded below. An indefinite \(A\) is unbounded below in every case.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(A\) symmetric,
\[
\nabla f(x) = A x + b, \qquad H_f(x) = A.
\]
The minimizer of a positive definite quadratic is \(x^\star = -A^{-1} b\), and
\[
f(x^\star) = c - \tfrac12 b^T A^{-1} b.
\]
The quadratic is coercive exactly when \(A\) is positive definite. Along a line, the restriction \(\tfrac12 a t^2 + g t\) with \(a > 0\) is minimized at \(t = -g/a\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 2)\), \(b = (-6, -2)\), and \(c = 29\). The system \(A x = -b\) reads \((2x, 2y) = (6, 2)\), so the minimizer is \((3, 1)\). The Hessian is positive definite, and there are no other candidates.

The solved quadratic floor is 19. One check is the value formula: \(A^{-1} b = (-3, -1)\), the dot product \(b^T A^{-1} b\) equals 20, and \(29 - 10 = 19\). The direct substitution \(9 + 1 - 18 - 2 + 29\) gives the same number. Changing \(c\) would shift the floor and would leave the minimizer where it is.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Positive semidefinite is not enough for existence. The function \(\tfrac12 x^2 + y\) has a positive semidefinite Hessian and is unbounded below, because the linear term in \(y\) never meets a restoring force. The false theorem is "convex implies the minimum is attained." Convexity supplies the tangent lower bound. Attainment is the column-space condition, or coercivity. A second mistake is to keep a factor of one half in the gradient after it was already used to simplify the derivative of the quadratic term. A third is to read eigenvalues of an unsymmetric matrix and call them the curvature.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Linear least squares is this quadratic with Hessian twice a Gram matrix, and the normal equations are \(A x = -b\) in that notation. An exact line search on a quadratic restricts the function to a line and uses the one-dimensional minimizer \(-g/a\). A convex quadratic with linear constraints is the model behind a support-vector objective once the constraints are restored.
